title: Irradiation Effects in Zirconium Nuclear Fuel Cladding Tubes Investigated by Atom Probe Tomography
content: In a light water nuclear reactor, uranium dioxide fuel pellets are contained inside long thin-walled tubes made of zirconium (Zr) alloys. The main reason for using Zr-alloys is the very low cross-section of Zr for thermal neutrons. In addition, they exhibit good resistance to water corrosion [1]. The neutron exposure results in significant irradiation damage during the lifetime (a few years) of the cladding tubes [2], with fluences reaching up to a few tens of dpa (displacements per atom). This results in irradiation growth and creep [3]. In many cases, the corrosion rate increases after a few years, a phenomenon called break-away corrosion, which also results in an increase in hydrogen pick-up and hydride formation [4]. In this work, cladding tubes from boiling water reactors have been studied using atom probe tomography (APT), a technique that can reveal microstructural changes on the nanometer level, with the aim of understanding the behavior of the various alloying elements and their impact on break-away corrosion.
